text: A boy goes to his idol
and says: “Sir, I'll work for you for *free*.”
And the answer comes: “*No.*”
That boy was *Warren Buffett*.
Today we'll see how, after *rejection*, *fear*
and one *big mistake*, he still made his own way.
Haven't seen Part 1? The link is in the description.
And if you're new, *subscribe* now:
this series will change the way you think.
After the Harvard rejection, 19-year-old Warren read a book:
*The Intelligent Investor*,
written by *Benjamin Graham*.
The book had one simple idea:
a share is not just a ticker,
it's a *piece of a business*.
Understand its *real value*,
and buy when the market is selling it *cheap*.
Warren felt as if someone had switched on a light in his mind.
He found out that Graham taught at *Columbia University*.
He applied right away,
got admission,
and reached his *guru*.
While studying at Columbia, Warren noticed that his guru Graham was the chairman of an insurance company, *GEICO*.
His curiosity woke up. One Saturday, he took a train to Washington
and knocked on GEICO's office door.
The office was closed. There was only a guard.
Warren asked: “Is there anyone who can explain the business to me?”
Upstairs, a senior executive, *Lorimer Davidson*, was at work.
He explained the insurance business to this unknown boy for *4 hours*.
That same curiosity later made GEICO one of Buffett's *favourite companies*.
Lesson: if you want to learn, *knock on the door*,
even on a Saturday. After graduation, Warren made Graham an offer:
“I'll work at your firm *without salary*.”
Graham *refused*.
Warren went back to Omaha
and started selling stocks at his father's firm.
But there was one problem.
Warren was terrified of *public speaking*.
Speaking in front of people, his hands would shake.
So what did he do? He paid *$100* and joined Dale Carnegie's public speaking course.
Later, Buffett himself said
it was the *most important degree* of his life.
And finally, in *1954*, Graham offered him a job.
Persistence *paid off*.
Friends, if you're also afraid of speaking on stage,
like this video and write in the comments:
“The only way to beat fear is to *face it*.”
In *1956*, Graham retired.
Now Warren had two paths:
a job in New York, or go back to Omaha and start his own business.
He chose *Omaha*.
At just *26*, he started the *Buffett Partnership*.
Where did the money come from? Family and friends:
And Warren's own share?
He worked from a small room in his house.
No big office, no big staff.
Only annual reports,
numbers and *discipline*.
Over the next 13 years, his partnership left the *Dow Jones* far behind.
Now comes Warren's *biggest mistake*.
In *1962*, he started buying shares of a sinking textile mill.
Its name: *Berkshire Hathaway*.
The plan was simple: buy cheap,
sell at a small profit. The company's boss first promised a deal at one price,
then cleverly offered a *lower* price.
Warren got *angry*.
In anger, he bought more shares and took *control* of the company.
The problem: the textile business was *sinking*.
Later, Buffett himself admitted:
“This was my *most expensive mistake*.”
A decision made in *anger*.
But look at fate: this same sinking company later became one of the *biggest companies* in the world.
How? We'll see that in *Part 3*.
In *1959*, Warren met *Charlie Munger*.
Charlie told him: “Warren, stop buying cheap things.
Buy a *wonderful company* at a *fair price*.”
This one line completely changed Buffett's way of investing.
And in *1969*, when everyone in the market was going crazy, Warren shocked everyone:
he *closed* his successful partnership.
Why? Because he couldn't find anything *cheap* in the market.
He didn't want to run with the crowd.
Today's lessons: to learn, *knock on the door*.
*Fear* can be trained.
And never take a decision in *anger*.
